head.citation-title: High-gravity intensified carbonation of larger steel slag particles: Dual-path CO2 mineralization and valorization in sustainable construction materials
head.abstracts: © 2025 Elsevier Ltd.Carbonation technology represents a promising strategy for the sustainable utilization of steel slag. This study investigates high-gravity (higee) intensified carbonation of large-particle steel slag (0.15-1.18 mm) as a dual-functional approach for CO2 sequestration and construction material valorization. Using a rotating packed bed (RPB), the higee process achieved equivalent carbonation levels to 60-minute traditional aqueous methods within 1 minute, with net negative emissions of -6.8 kg CO2-eq/ton slag. Mechanistic analysis revealed that the higee environment effectively separated steel slag slurry into water-film-coated particles and calcium-rich micro-droplets, enabling in-situ CaCO3 layer formation on particles as fine aggregates and ex-situ CaCO3 precipitation (80 % purity) as supplementary cementitious materials (SCMs). While reduced particle size enhanced CO2 uptake and ex-situ CaCO3 yield, higher RPB speeds compromised purity via impurity introduction. Life cycle and cost analyses demonstrated 36 %-40 % lower energy consumption and 52.1 CNY/ton economic benefit compared to conventional methods. Furthermore, mortar incorporating carbonated slag exhibited 164.6 % compressive strength enhancement due to interfacial transition zone densification. This work provides a techno-economically viable pathway for industrial-scale CO2 utilization and steel slag upcycling.

coredata.dc:description: Carbonation technology represents a promising strategy for the sustainable utilization of steel slag. This study investigates high-gravity (higee) intensified carbonation of large-particle steel slag (0.15-1.18 mm) as a dual-functional approach for CO2 sequestration and construction material valorization. Using a rotating packed bed (RPB), the higee process achieved equivalent carbonation levels to 60-minute traditional aqueous methods within 1 minute, with net negative emissions of -6.8 kg CO2-eq/ton slag. Mechanistic analysis revealed that the higee environment effectively separated steel slag slurry into water-film-coated particles and calcium-rich micro-droplets, enabling in-situ CaCO3 layer formation on particles as fine aggregates and ex-situ CaCO3 precipitation (80 % purity) as supplementary cementitious materials (SCMs). While reduced particle size enhanced CO2 uptake and ex-situ CaCO3 yield, higher RPB speeds compromised purity via impurity introduction. Life cycle and cost analyses demonstrated 36 %-40 % lower energy consumption and 52.1 CNY/ton economic benefit compared to conventional methods. Furthermore, mortar incorporating carbonated slag exhibited 164.6 % compressive strength enhancement due to interfacial transition zone densification. This work provides a techno-economically viable pathway for industrial-scale CO2 utilization and steel slag upcycling.
coredata.dc:title: High-gravity intensified carbonation of larger steel slag particles: Dual-path CO2 mineralization and valorization in sustainable construction materials
